newsitem.title: USA: ValuJet says will continue to be low-fare airline.
newsitem.headline: ValuJet says will continue to be low-fare airline.

text.p: ValuJet President Lewis Jordan said on Friday the airline would still offer "affordable" fares despite the costs of complying with Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) requirements imposed to permit it to resume operations.

In television interviews on NBC and ABC, Jordan said the airline would rely on only two outside contractors for heavy maintenance. It had redone its training programmes and maintenance manuals as well as hire a senior vice president for maintenance.
"We conserved cash during this difficult period of time so we come back very strong," he told ABC's Good Morning America.
He said the Department of Transportation reviewed ValuJet's balance sheet and determined it was strong enough financially to resume flying. "We have a lot of money in the bank."

"We will pass along the same affordable fares that the public wants," he added. "We have over $200 million in cash. Even if we spend $50 million on the shutdown that leaves us with a lot of cash," he said.
Atlanta-based ValuJet was grounded on June 17 after a heightened safety inspection of the carrier following a crash in the Florida Everglades on May 11 that killed 110 people.
The FAA said on Thursday it had returned the carrier's operating certificate after a review found ValuJet to have corrected the maintenance and operation failings that led to the grounding.

After a period for government review of any response to the proposed flight approval, the airline could fly nine planes at first and up to 15 over the next several days. Before it was grounded ValuJet flew 51 aircraft.
The shutdown and the costs of changes instituted at the airline will be a one-time charge against expenses, Jordan said.

In response to concerns the company could not make a profit while following stricter safety rules and holding down fares, Jordan said: "We cut out hot meals and frequent flyer programmes. We don't do company cars and we don't do fancy furniture, but we spend all the money necessary for top-notch maintenance programmes and that is exactly what the FAA has just found."
